question: to the Commission Jean-Paul Garraud (PfE) Subject:
Montenegro’s accession: the EUR 3.2 billion cost to EU citizens

The Commission estimates that Montenegro’s accession on 1 January 2028 would result in approximately EUR 3.2 billion in additional EU spending between 2028 and 2034. This sum would fund, among other things, the country’s economic and regional development, gradual access to EU agricultural subsidies, border controls, security and competitiveness. The Commission also envisages an additional EUR 442 million in additional administrative spending for the EU institutions. This is the estimate at a point when only 16 of the 33 chapters in the accession negotiations have been provisionally closed. 1.
What would be the real net cost of this accession, after deducting Montenegro’s future contribution to the EU budget and the pre-accession assistance that it would no longer receive?
Would this additional spending be funded by raising Member States’ contributions, by reducing the funding currently allocated to Member States, or through new EU resources?

Before negotiations conclude, will the Commission publish a study detailing the impacts of this accession on the budget of each Member State, the composition of the European Parliament, the votes in the Council and institution staffing levels?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (24.9.2026) The Commission communication1 sets out the gross budgetary impact of Montenegro’s prospective accession. The net cost will depend on Montenegro’s future contribution to the EU budget, to be set once EU acquis’ Chapter 33 (Financial and Budgetary Provisions)2 negotiations close. To partially offset the additional expenditure, the Commission proposes to transfer Montenegro’s allocation under the proposed Europe Pillar of the Global Europe instrument3, between budget headings, within its proposal for the next Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF) 2028–20344. The package ensures that Member States are not negatively impacted, so the additional expenditure is not intended to be met by reducing the funding foreseen for the EU-27. The introduction of new own resources would strengthen the sustainability of revenues needed to support key EU priorities, all without adding undue burden onto Member States contributions. These priorities include not only the funding of a larger EU but also other key priorities such as security and competitiveness. The Commission is preparing pre-enlargement policy reviews to ensure the EU is politically, institutionally and financially prepared for a larger membership, taking into account that the Treaties already offer possibilities to adapt its governance to an enlarged EU. Definitive figures cannot be provided at this stage, pending the outcome of negotiations on the next MFF and the Own Resources Decision5.
